title: SQL from basics to advanced
scopeHtml: Scope: joins, aggregation, subqueries, CTEs, window functions, pagination, with exercises and answers.

notes.title: The practice schema used in this file
notes.html:
All examples use one small shop schema so you can paste it into Postgres (or MySQL with tiny changes) and run everything.

CREATE TABLE customers (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text, city text, signup date);
CREATE TABLE orders    (id int PRIMARY KEY, customer_id int REFERENCES customers, status text, total int, created date);
CREATE TABLE products  (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text, price int);
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id int REFERENCES orders, product_id int REFERENCES products, qty int,
                          PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id));

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Asha','Pune','2025-01-10'),(2,'Ben','Delhi','2025-02-01'),
                             (3,'Chitra','Pune','2025-03-15'),(4,'Dev',NULL,'2025-04-01');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,'paid',500,'2025-05-01'),(11,1,'paid',300,'2025-05-09'),
                          (12,2,'paid',900,'2025-05-10'),(13,3,'refunded',200,'2025-06-01');
INSERT INTO products VALUES (100,'pen',10),(101,'book',150),(102,'bag',700);
INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (10,100,5),(10,102,1),(11,101,2),(12,102,1),(12,101,1),(13,100,20);

Why learn SQL by one schema. Interviewers ask "write a query" on a whiteboard schema like this; the skill is reading a requirement, picking tables, then picking the right join and grouping.

Everyday analogy. A practice kitchen with the same five ingredients so you can focus on the recipes.

Common interview traps.

  • Not asking for the schema, keys and whether columns can be NULL before writing.
  • Writing a query that is right on 4 rows but wrong on edge cases (customers with no orders).

notes.title: Logical order of a SELECT
notes.html:
SQL is written in one order but evaluated in another. Knowing the evaluation order explains most "why can't I use that alias there" errors.

Written:    SELECT  FROM  WHERE  GROUP BY  HAVING  ORDER BY  LIMIT
Evaluated:  FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> window functions
            -> SELECT (aliases defined) -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT

So WHERE cannot use a SELECT alias or an aggregate; HAVING filters groups after aggregation; ORDER BY can use aliases.

-- Revenue per city, only cities above 500, biggest first
SELECT c.city, sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'         -- row filter, before grouping
GROUP BY c.city
HAVING sum(o.total) > 500       -- group filter, after grouping
ORDER BY revenue DESC           -- alias allowed here
LIMIT 10;

Result for the sample data: Pune 800 (500+300, paid only), Delhi 900. Delhi 900 first, then Pune 800.

Worked example. Filtering paid orders in WHERE (not HAVING) shrinks 10M rows to 2M before the expensive grouping; put row filters in WHERE whenever possible.

MySQL differences. MySQL historically allowed non-aggregated columns in GROUP BY queries (ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off); modern 5.7+ defaults it on. Postgres always rejected such queries unless the column is functionally dependent on the grouped key.

Everyday analogy. Cooking: you gather ingredients (FROM), discard bad ones (WHERE), group them, taste the groups (HAVING), then plate (SELECT) and serve in order (ORDER BY).

Common interview traps.

  • Using aggregates in WHERE.
  • LIMIT without ORDER BY (arbitrary rows).
  • Thinking SELECT runs first.

notes.title: Joins: inner, outer, cross, self
notes.html:
A join combines rows from two tables where a condition matches.

Join Keeps
INNER JOIN Only matching pairs
LEFT JOIN All left rows, matched right rows or NULLs
RIGHT JOIN Mirror of left (rarely needed)
FULL JOIN All rows from both sides
CROSS JOIN Every pair (m x n rows) 
-- All customers, with order count (Dev has none)
SELECT c.name, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY c.name;
--  Asha 2 | Ben 1 | Chitra 1 | Dev 0
-- Customers who NEVER ordered (anti-join)
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;          -- Dev
-- Self join: pairs of customers in the same city
SELECT a.name, b.name FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id;   -- Asha, Chitra

The classic bug. A filter on the right table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join: LEFT JOIN orders o ... WHERE o.status = 'paid' drops customers with no orders. Put it in the ON clause: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'.

Worked example. Joining customers (1M) to orders (10M) on an indexed customer_id returns 10M rows, not 1M: one row per match. Counting customers after that join without DISTINCT overcounts (the fan-out problem).

Industry view. Join strategy (nested loop, hash, merge) is chosen by the planner; see file 05. MySQL had no hash join until 8.0.18, so older schemas relied heavily on indexes for joins.

Everyday analogy. Matching a list of guests with a list of RSVPs: inner join shows people who RSVPed; left join shows everyone, blank where no RSVP.

Common interview traps.

  • Filtering the right table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN.
  • Fan-out: summing a parent column after joining to children.
  • Forgetting MySQL has no FULL JOIN (emulate with UNION of left and right).

notes.title: Aggregation, GROUP BY, HAVING, DISTINCT
notes.html:
Aggregation collapses many rows into one per group: count, sum, avg, min, max, string_agg (MySQL GROUP_CONCAT), array_agg.

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, sum(total) AS total, round(avg(total),1) AS avg_total
FROM orders GROUP BY status;
-- paid 3 1700 566.7 | refunded 1 200 200.0

Useful details:

  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-null values.
  • FILTER (WHERE ...) (Postgres) gives conditional aggregates; MySQL uses SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
  • GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE produce subtotals in one pass.
SELECT customer_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')     AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'refunded') AS refunded
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

SELECT c.city, o.status, sum(o.total)
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP (c.city, o.status);   -- adds per-city and grand total rows

Worked example. GROUP BY on 50M rows with 1,000 distinct keys: hash aggregate needs memory for 1,000 groups (tiny) and one pass. With 50M distinct keys it needs gigabytes and may spill to disk (work_mem default 4 MB in Postgres; EXPLAIN shows Disk: in HashAggregate on Postgres 13+).

Everyday analogy. Sorting receipts into piles by month and writing a total on each pile.

Common interview traps.

  • SELECT name, count(*) ... GROUP BY city (selecting a non-grouped column).
  • AVG of a column with NULLs divides by non-null count only.
  • Using HAVING where WHERE would be cheaper.

notes.title: Subqueries, EXISTS, IN, correlated queries
notes.html:
A subquery is a query inside another. Types: scalar (one value), row/list (for IN), table (in FROM), and correlated (refers to the outer row, re-evaluated conceptually per outer row).

-- Scalar: orders bigger than average
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE total > (SELECT avg(total) FROM orders);

-- Semi-join: customers with at least one paid order
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid');

-- Anti-join, NULL safe
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- Correlated: each customer's latest order
SELECT c.name, (SELECT max(created) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS last_order
FROM customers c;

EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN. Modern planners (Postgres, MySQL 8) usually rewrite IN and EXISTS to a semi-join, giving the same plan. NOT IN is different: a single NULL in the list makes it return nothing, so always prefer NOT EXISTS. A join can duplicate rows; EXISTS never does.

Worked example. Customer table 1M, orders 10M with index on orders(customer_id). EXISTS does at most 1M index probes (stop at first hit) rather than materialising 10M rows. A correlated scalar subquery in SELECT without an index becomes 1M sequential scans: a classic accidental O(n^2).

Everyday analogy. "Is there anyone in the room named Priya?" You stop looking the moment you find one.

Common interview traps.

  • NOT IN with NULLs.
  • Correlated subquery on an unindexed column.
  • Joining then DISTINCT to simulate semi-join (slow, hides fan-out).

notes.title: CTEs and recursive queries
notes.html:
A CTE (WITH name AS (...)) names a subquery so you can read the query top to bottom. In Postgres 12+, a non-recursive CTE referenced once is inlined (treated like a subquery); referenced more than once, or with MATERIALIZED, it is computed once and stored. Before 12, CTEs were always materialised, acting as an optimisation fence.

WITH paid AS (
  SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS spent FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, p.spent FROM paid p JOIN customers c ON c.id = p.customer_id
WHERE p.spent > 400;       -- Asha 800, Ben 900

Recursive CTE walks hierarchies (org charts, category trees, threads):

CREATE TABLE emp (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text, boss_id int);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'CEO',NULL),(2,'VP',1),(3,'Lead',2),(4,'Dev',3);

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, boss_id, 1 AS depth FROM emp WHERE id = 4      -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.boss_id, c.depth + 1
  FROM emp e JOIN chain c ON e.id = c.boss_id                      -- step
)
SELECT * FROM chain;       -- Dev(1), Lead(2), VP(3), CEO(4)

Safety: cyclic data loops forever. Add a depth limit (WHERE depth < 20) or track visited ids (CYCLE clause exists in Postgres 14+). MySQL supports recursive CTEs from 8.0 (default cte_max_recursion_depth 1000).

Worked example. Category tree with 50k nodes, depth 8: recursive CTE runs 8 iterations, each joining the frontier with an index on boss_id/parent_id, in milliseconds. The alternative, one query per level from the app, costs 8 round trips.

Industry examples. Comment threads (Reddit-style), BOM (bill of materials) explosion, and permission inheritance are typical recursive CTE uses. Very large graphs move to graph stores or materialised paths (ltree in Postgres).

Everyday analogy. Asking "who is your boss?" repeatedly until you reach someone with no boss.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing CTEs are always materialised (changed in Postgres 12).
  • Recursive CTE without a termination guard on possibly cyclic data.
  • Using UNION (dedupes, slower) when UNION ALL is enough.

notes.title: Window functions
notes.html:
A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row, WITHOUT collapsing them (unlike GROUP BY). Syntax: func() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame).

Families:

  • Ranking: row_number(), rank() (ties share, gaps follow), dense_rank() (ties share, no gaps), ntile(n).
  • Offset: lag(col, n), lead(col, n), first_value, last_value.
  • Aggregate as window: sum(x) OVER (...) for running totals, avg for moving averages.
-- Each customer's orders with running total and previous order amount
SELECT customer_id, id, created, total,
       sum(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created) AS running,
       lag(total)  OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created) AS prev_total,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created DESC) AS rn
FROM orders;
-- Asha: 10 -> running 500, prev NULL, rn 2 | 11 -> running 800, prev 500, rn 1

Top-N per group is the interview favourite:

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT o.*, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC) rn FROM orders o
) t WHERE rn = 1;          -- biggest order per customer

Frames. With ORDER BY, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (peers with equal order values are included together). last_value surprises people because of this default; specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Moving 7-day average: avg(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

Worked example. Daily revenue 365 rows: sum(rev) OVER (ORDER BY d) gives YTD without a self-join (which would be 365 x 365/2 = 66k comparisons). Window evaluation sorts once (O(n log n)) then streams. MySQL supports windows from 8.0.

Everyday analogy. A leaderboard where everyone stays on the list, but each row also shows rank and the gap to the person above.

Common interview traps.

  • rank vs dense_rank vs row_number with ties.
  • Filtering on a window function in WHERE (not allowed; wrap in a subquery or CTE).
  • Forgetting the default frame for last_value.

notes.title: Set operations, CASE, and handy patterns
notes.html:
Set operations combine query results with the same column shape: UNION (dedupe), UNION ALL (keep all, faster), INTERSECT, EXCEPT (MySQL gained INTERSECT/EXCEPT in 8.0.31).

-- Cities that have customers but whose customers placed no refunded order
SELECT city FROM customers
EXCEPT
SELECT c.city FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id WHERE o.status='refunded';

CASE is SQL's if/else; use it for pivots and bucketing:

SELECT customer_id,
  sum(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN total ELSE 0 END)     AS paid_amt,
  sum(CASE WHEN status='refunded' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS refund_amt
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

Pagination. OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20 reads and discards 100,000 rows; cost grows with page number. Use keyset pagination:

SELECT id, created FROM orders
WHERE (created, id) < ('2025-05-10', 12)
ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;      -- needs index on (created, id)

Upsert. Postgres: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET .... MySQL: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. Find duplicates: SELECT email, count(*) FROM u GROUP BY email HAVING count(*) > 1. Nth highest: SELECT DISTINCT total FROM orders ORDER BY total DESC OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1 or dense_rank().

Worked example. Page 5,000 of a feed with OFFSET: 100,000 rows scanned, ~50 ms to seconds; keyset: ~1 ms regardless of depth. Twitter, Slack and Stripe APIs use cursor (keyset) pagination for exactly this reason.

Everyday analogy. A bookmark in a book versus counting 5,000 pages from the cover every time.

Common interview traps.

  • OFFSET for deep pagination.
  • UNION when UNION ALL suffices.
  • Keyset pagination without a unique tiebreaker column (skips or repeats rows).

notes.title: Exercises
notes.html:
Try each before reading the answer. Use the practice schema above.

  1. Names of customers with more than one paid order.
  2. Total revenue (paid only) per city, including cities with zero revenue.
  3. The most expensive order per customer (ties: lowest id).
  4. Customers who bought a bag (product 102) but never a pen.
  5. For each order, the running total of the customer's paid spend ordered by date.
  6. The second highest order total.
  7. Products never sold.
  8. Month-over-month revenue change.

notes.title: Exercise answers
notes.html:
-- 1
SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id, c.name HAVING count(*) > 1;           -- Asha

-- 2 (LEFT JOIN with the filter in ON keeps zero-revenue cities)
SELECT c.city, coalesce(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid'
GROUP BY c.city;                  -- Pune 800, Delhi 900, NULL 0

-- 3
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, id, total       -- Postgres only
FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, total DESC, id;
-- portable:  row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC, id)

-- 4
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id
              WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND i.product_id=102)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id
              WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND i.product_id=100);   -- Ben

-- 5
SELECT id, customer_id, created,
       sum(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created) AS running
FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

-- 6
SELECT DISTINCT total FROM orders ORDER BY total DESC OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1;   -- 500

-- 7
SELECT p.name FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id
WHERE i.product_id IS NULL;       -- none in sample data

-- 8
WITH m AS (SELECT date_trunc('month', created) AS mon, sum(total) AS rev
           FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY 1)
SELECT mon, rev, rev - lag(rev) OVER (ORDER BY mon) AS change FROM m;

Why these matter. Q1 (HAVING), Q2 (LEFT JOIN trap), Q3 and Q5 (windows), Q4 (semi and anti-join), Q6 (dense ranking or OFFSET), Q7 (anti-join), Q8 (CTE plus lag) cover most "SQL round" patterns at product companies.

Everyday analogy. Finger exercises: you practise a few scales until the shapes are automatic.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering without testing on the empty and tied cases.
  • Using DISTINCT to hide a join fan-out.
  • Not stating the dialect when using DISTINCT ON, FILTER or LIMIT.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Evaluation order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, windows, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
  • LEFT JOIN plus right-table filter in WHERE silently becomes an inner join; put it in ON.
  • Prefer EXISTS / NOT EXISTS over IN / NOT IN when NULLs are possible.
  • Aggregate collapses rows; window functions keep rows and add computed columns.
  • Know row_number vs rank vs dense_rank, lag/lead, and window frames.
  • CTEs are inlined in Postgres 12+ unless referenced twice or MATERIALIZED; recursive CTEs need a termination guard.
  • Use keyset pagination, not deep OFFSET.
  • Dialect notes: MySQL 8 has CTEs and windows, no FULL JOIN, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, GROUP_CONCAT.

questions.promptHtml: In what order does SQL logically evaluate a SELECT, and why can't you use a column alias in WHERE?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A mental model that explains most "why does this error" and "why is this slow" questions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The written order is not the evaluation order. Logically it is FROM and JOINs, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions, SELECT (where aliases are born), DISTINCT, ORDER BY, then LIMIT. WHERE runs before SELECT, so an alias defined in SELECT does not exist yet. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can use aliases."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> WINDOW -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT

Consequences:

  • WHERE cannot reference aggregates or window results; use HAVING for aggregates, a subquery/CTE for windows.
  • HAVING sees groups; WHERE sees rows, so filter rows in WHERE to shrink work before grouping.
  • This is the logical model. The optimizer may reorder joins and push filters down as long as results match.
  • MySQL and Postgres allow aliases in GROUP BY/ORDER BY as an extension; not in WHERE.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS spent          -- alias born here
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'                             -- row filter, before grouping
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING sum(total) > 500                           -- group filter
ORDER BY spent DESC                               -- alias usable
LIMIT 10;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• WHERE spent > 500 using an alias.
  • Putting row filters in HAVING (computes groups you throw away).
  • Thinking LIMIT applies before ORDER BY.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a window function appear in WHERE? -> No; wrap in a subquery/CTE.
  2. Does the engine really run in that order? -> Logically yes; physically the planner reorders.
  3. Why does SELECT DISTINCT a ORDER BY b fail? -> b is not in the projected set after DISTINCT.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists clauses. The senior uses the order to explain errors and to decide whether a filter belongs in WHERE or HAVING for performance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A report with filters in HAVING grouped 80M rows instead of 2M, taking 6 minutes instead of 20 seconds.

questions.promptHtml: Explain INNER, LEFT, FULL and CROSS joins. What changes when a filter is in ON versus WHERE for a LEFT JOIN?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundational; the ON vs WHERE point catches many.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "INNER keeps only matching pairs. LEFT keeps every left row, filling NULLs when nothing matches. FULL keeps unmatched rows from both sides. CROSS is every combination. For a LEFT JOIN, a condition in ON decides what counts as a match and keeps unmatched left rows; the same condition in WHERE runs after the join and removes NULL-extended rows, turning it into an inner join."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
customers: Asha, Ben, Dev        orders: Asha(2), Ben(1)
LEFT JOIN -> Asha, Asha, Ben, Dev(NULL order)
  • ON filter on the right table: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' still returns Dev.
  • WHERE filter on the right table: WHERE o.status='paid' drops Dev (NULL status is not 'paid').
  • CROSS JOIN size: m x n. 10k x 10k = 100M rows; a missing join condition does this by accident.
  • Self join: join a table to itself with aliases (employee and manager).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT c.name, count(o.id) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.name;       -- Dev appears with 0

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Right-table predicate in WHERE for a LEFT JOIN.
  • Missing join condition giving a cartesian product.
  • Using count(*) instead of count(o.id) after a LEFT JOIN.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to find customers without orders? -> LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL or NOT EXISTS.
  2. Does join order matter in the query text? -> Not for inner joins (planner reorders); matters for readability and for outer joins semantically.
  3. What is a semi-join? -> Rows from the left that have a match, without duplicating from the right (EXISTS/IN).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer draws Venn diagrams. The senior explains matching vs filtering and the NULL-extension effect.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard "customers with their paid orders" silently dropped customers with none after someone moved a condition to WHERE.

questions.contextHtml:
Task: "for each city, number of customers and number of orders". Query written:

SELECT c.city, count(*) AS customers, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.city;
-- result with the sample data: Pune | 3 | 3   Delhi | 1 | 1   NULL | 1 | 0
-- expected:                    Pune | 2 | 3   Delhi | 1 | 1   NULL | 1 | 0

Sample: Asha (Pune, 2 orders), Chitra (Pune, 1 order), Ben (Delhi, 1 order), Dev (no city, 0 orders). A teammate suggests DISTINCT.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the customers column wrong, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: SELECT DISTINCT on the whole row, which removes legitimate rows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should customers with NULL city be a separate group? Can a customer have duplicate names? Is customers.id unique?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I hand-check with sample data first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The LEFT JOIN multiplies customer rows by order count (fan-out), so count(*) counts joined rows, not customers.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the query without GROUP BY and look at Asha appearing twice.
  5. Root cause: count(*) counts rows after the join. Asha has 2 orders so she is counted twice.
  6. Fix:
SELECT c.city, count(DISTINCT c.id) AS customers, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.city;

Alternative: aggregate orders per customer first, then join, which avoids fan-out for several metrics. 7. Prevention: Test with a customer that has multiple orders and one with none. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: count(DISTINCT) is slower on large data; pre-aggregating in a subquery is better with several measures. Not whole-row DISTINCT.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does the NULL city show up as its own group? -> GROUP BY treats NULLs as equal.
  • Add revenue per city? -> Pre-aggregate orders by customer or you will multiply sums by item rows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An exec dashboard overstated active customers by 30% because of a one-to-many join feeding count(*).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Random DISTINCT.
  • Hire: Names fan-out and uses count(DISTINCT id).
  • Strong hire: Also pre-aggregates, and tests with multi-row and zero-row cases.

questions.contextHtml:
A "customers and their May orders" report must show all customers, including those with no May orders. Output has 3,100 rows while the customers table has 5,000.

SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created >= '2025-05-01' AND o.created < '2025-06-01';

The data team says "the join must be broken, let's use FULL JOIN". Red herring: orders has 90M rows and a recent index rebuild.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and fix it, including an index.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switches to FULL JOIN or removes the date filter.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should customers without May orders appear with NULL? (yes). Are dates timestamps or dates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-run corrected query for the report.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: WHERE on the outer table kills NULL-extended rows; the 1,900 missing customers are those with no May order.
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT count(*) FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.created >= '2025-05-01' AND o.created < '2025-06-01') returns about 1,900.
  5. Root cause: After the LEFT JOIN, unmatched rows have o.created = NULL; the WHERE predicate is UNKNOWN and removes them, so the query behaves like an INNER JOIN.
  6. Fix: Move the date predicate into ON:
SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  AND o.created >= '2025-05-01' AND o.created < '2025-06-01';
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created);
  1. Prevention: Code review rule: no right-table column in WHERE for a LEFT JOIN unless it is IS NULL.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not FULL JOIN (adds orphan orders, wrong semantics). Half-open date range avoids a time-of-day bug at the month end.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Want only customers WITH May orders? -> Then INNER JOIN is the clearer intent.
  • Index choice? -> (customer_id, created) supports lookups by customer then range.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A churn report omitted inactive users for a year because of this exact WHERE-after-LEFT-JOIN.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Changes join type.
  • Hire: Moves predicate to ON.
  • Strong hire: Explains UNKNOWN filtering, index design, half-open range.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly job finds users to email: users who have never placed an order.

SELECT id, email FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);

For 2 years it returned about 40k rows. Today it returns 0 rows and the campaign did not send. No errors. Yesterday a new import path inserted 120 orders with user_id NULL (guest checkout). Red herring: the users table was vacuumed at the same time.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how do you write it safely and fast?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Maybe the import broke something" without knowing why one NULL empties the result.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can orders.user_id be NULL by design? How large is orders (rows)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-run with NOT EXISTS.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: NULL in the subquery list; plan change; permissions. First is consistent with "0 rows and no error".
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id IS NULL; returns 120.
  5. Root cause: x NOT IN (1,2,NULL) expands to x<>1 AND x<>2 AND x<>NULL, the last is UNKNOWN, so the whole predicate is never TRUE.
  6. Fix:
SELECT u.id, u.email FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id);
-- illustrative plan: Hash Anti Join (rows=40012)

Also enforce NOT NULL or a separate guest table if guests are not users. 7. Prevention: Lint to ban NOT IN (subquery); add a test with a NULL row. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL if duplicates make it slower to read; both are fine as anti-joins. NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and the planner turns it into an anti-join.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would NOT IN (literal list) have the same issue? -> Yes, if the list contains NULL.
  • Why does IN not have the problem? -> IN needs only one TRUE match; UNKNOWN for others does not matter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An unsubscribe job sent no suppression because one NULL appeared in the suppression list; an incident review banned NOT IN with subqueries.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot explain the zero rows.
  • Hire: Identifies NULL and uses NOT EXISTS.
  • Strong hire: Explains expansion, anti-join plan, constraint fix and lint.

questions.promptHtml: Differentiate ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK, and explain why last_value() often returns the wrong thing.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Window functions are common in senior SQL screens; ties and frames are the traps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "All three number rows within a partition by ORDER BY. ROW_NUMBER gives unique numbers even for ties, RANK gives ties the same number then skips, DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps. last_value surprises people because with an ORDER BY the default frame ends at the current row, so it returns the current row's value, not the partition's last."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Scores 100, 90, 90, 80:

row_number: 1 2 3 4     rank: 1 2 2 4     dense_rank: 1 2 2 3
  • ROW_NUMBER is nondeterministic among ties unless the ORDER BY includes a unique tiebreaker.
  • Default frame with ORDER BY: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW; RANGE includes peer rows (equal order values), ROWS counts physical rows.
  • To get the true last value: last_value(x) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING), or order DESC and use first_value.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SELECT customer_id, id, total,
  row_number() OVER w AS rn, rank() OVER w AS rk, dense_rank() OVER w AS dr,
  last_value(total) OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_total
FROM orders
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using ROW_NUMBER for "top 3 salaries" when ties should share.
  • Running totals with RANGE on non-unique order keys giving peer jumps.
  • Filtering a window function in WHERE.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Third highest distinct salary? -> dense_rank() = 3 in a subquery.
  2. Moving 7-day average? -> avg(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
  3. Difference between RANGE and ROWS with ties? -> RANGE groups peers; ROWS is physical.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer gives the three outputs. The senior adds determinism, frame defaults and ROWS vs RANGE.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "latest status" query used last_value with default frame and returned stale statuses for tied timestamps.

questions.contextHtml:
Product wants "the 3 most recent orders per customer" for a 2M-customer, 60M-order system. Current query:

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT o.*, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created DESC) rn FROM orders o
) t WHERE rn <= 3;

It takes 38 s (illustrative):

-- illustrative
WindowAgg  (actual time=21000..36000 rows=60000000)
  -> Sort (Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 4800000kB)

It runs per-request for one customer's page as ... WHERE customer_id = 42, yet someone also uses it for a nightly export of everyone.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds LIMIT 3 outside (wrong) or says "add RAM".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which query is on the request path? Is the export all customers or only active? Are ties on created possible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add WHERE customer_id = $1 inside for the request path; with the index it reads 3 rows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Full sort of 60M rows spilling to disk (4.8 GB). Missing composite index. Unneeded o.* width.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS); check \d orders indexes.
  5. Root cause: The window runs over every order and sorts all of them before filtering rn <= 3.
  6. Fix: Index orders (customer_id, created DESC).
  • Request path: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=$1 ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT 3;
  • Export: LATERAL top-N per customer:
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created DESC);
SELECT c.id, o.*
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT 3) o;
-- illustrative: 2M index probes, each reads 3 index entries, no big sort
  1. Prevention: Track queries with disk sorts (temp_files, log_temp_files).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The window version is fine for small tables or when most rows are needed. With heavy skew (a few customers have 1M orders) LATERAL stays fast. Add id as a tiebreaker for determinism.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 10x orders? -> The LATERAL plan scales with customers, not orders.
  • MySQL 5.7 (no window/lateral)? -> Upgrade; or use a correlated subquery with LIMIT via a join on rank subquery.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An export that took 45 minutes dropped to 3 with the LATERAL form and one composite index.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot read the plan.
  • Hire: Adds the composite index and filters by customer.
  • Strong hire: LATERAL for bulk, tiebreaker, discusses skew and temp files.

questions.contextHtml:
Finance reports revenue of $12.4M for May in the dashboard but the ledger says $8.1M. The dashboard query:

SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created) m, sum(o.total) AS revenue, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1;

Orders have on average 1.5 items. The change last week: an item-level "product category" filter was added by joining order_items. orders count in the dashboard is also inflated by about 50%. Red herring: refunds are in a separate table.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and explain how you would prevent it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames refunds or timezone, or adds DISTINCT to the SELECT.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is orders.total the whole order amount? Does the ledger count per order or per item? When did numbers diverge?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pull the dashboard tile or footnote it; report from a corrected query.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Row multiplication by the items join (12.4 / 8.1 is about 1.53, matching items per order). Refund exclusion would not scale by an item factor. Timezone shifts move rows between months, not multiply them.
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND created in May; vs the joined sum; SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT o.id) on the join.
  5. Root cause: orders.total is repeated once per matching item row, so sum(o.total) counts it 1.5x on average. The join changed the grain from order to item.
  6. Fix: Keep the grain consistent. Either aggregate items separately or use EXISTS for the filter:
SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created) m, sum(o.total) revenue, count(*) orders
FROM orders o
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i JOIN products p ON p.id=i.product_id
              WHERE i.order_id = o.id AND p.category = 'books')
GROUP BY 1;

For item-level metrics sum i.qty*i.unit_price instead of o.total. 7. Prevention: Reconciliation test: dashboard total must equal ledger total within tolerance; a rule "state the grain of every query". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not sum(DISTINCT o.total) (collapses legitimately equal totals) and not DISTINCT on the whole row. EXISTS avoids duplicate rows entirely.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need both order-level and item-level numbers? -> Pre-aggregate each in subqueries, then join on order_id.
  • Why was it correct before? -> Without the items join the grain was one row per order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A partner commission report overpaid by 38% for a quarter because a join to line items inflated order totals.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Guesses refunds/timezone.
  • Hire: Identifies fan-out and fixes with EXISTS or pre-aggregation.
  • Strong hire: Uses the ratio as evidence, defines grain, adds reconciliation checks.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use EXISTS, IN or a JOIN to filter rows by related data? Are they equivalent?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of semi-joins, duplicates and NULL behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "For 'rows that have a match', EXISTS and IN are semi-joins and return each outer row once. A JOIN returns one row per match, so it can duplicate rows and needs DISTINCT, which hides fan-out. Planners usually give the same plan for IN and EXISTS. NOT EXISTS and NOT IN are not equivalent: NOT IN returns nothing if the list contains a NULL."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
EXISTS : for each outer row, stop at the first match
IN     : build/hash the inner set, probe (planner often converts to semi-join)
JOIN   : produce all matching pairs
  • Postgres and MySQL 8 convert IN (subquery) and EXISTS into semi-joins; legacy MySQL 5.5 ran IN as a dependent subquery and was slow.
  • Use EXISTS when the inner side is large and indexed on the correlation column: 1M customers x index probe is cheap.
  • Use JOIN when you need columns from the inner table.
  • For anti-joins prefer NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- customers with a paid order
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid');
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='paid');
-- illustrative plan for both: Hash Semi Join

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• JOIN ... DISTINCT as a semi-join substitute.
  • NOT IN with nullable subquery column.
  • Assuming EXISTS is always faster than IN on modern engines.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. SELECT 1 vs SELECT * in EXISTS? -> No difference; the select list is ignored.
  2. Which is better on correlated large subqueries without index? -> None; add the index first.
  3. How do you check? -> Compare EXPLAIN for Semi Join vs SubPlan.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "EXISTS is faster". The senior says the planner often makes them equal and focuses on duplicates and NULL semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A DISTINCT after a join hid a 30x fan-out and cost 12 s on an endpoint; EXISTS cut it to 80 ms.

questions.contextHtml:
An admin export API paginates GET /orders?page=N with ORDER BY created DESC OFFSET (N-1)*50 LIMIT 50. 120M rows. A partner script crawls pages 1 to 2.4M. DB CPU rises to 90%, p99 for the API goes from 40 ms to 6 s, replicas lag. Plan at page 400,000 (illustrative):

-- illustrative
Limit  (actual time=2100..2100 rows=50)
  -> Index Scan Backward using orders_created_idx (actual time=0.03..2095 rows=20000050)

Some rows are also missing or repeated between pages because orders are inserted constantly. Red herring: the connection pool is only 40% used.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it slow and unstable and how do you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index on created" (already exists) or raise the pool size.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must clients jump to arbitrary page numbers? Is there a stable sort key? Can we cap or rate-limit partners?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rate-limit the partner key and cap page at, say, 1,000; return 400 beyond.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: OFFSET scans and discards N rows (20M here); non-unique created plus inserts shifting offsets; also a missing tiebreaker.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) rows read vs returned; query logs by page parameter.
  5. Root cause: OFFSET is O(N) per request, total crawl O(N^2). Offsets are positions, so concurrent inserts shift pages and cause skips and duplicates.
  6. Fix: Keyset (cursor) pagination with a unique sort key:
CREATE INDEX orders_created_id_idx ON orders (created DESC, id DESC);
SELECT id, created, total FROM orders
WHERE (created, id) < ($1, $2)          -- cursor from the last row
ORDER BY created DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50;   -- ~1 ms at any depth

Return an opaque next_cursor; offer page only for small ranges. 7. Prevention: API guideline: cursor pagination for any unbounded list; alert on queries scanning many more rows than returned. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keyset cannot jump to page 5,000; document it. Not COUNT(*) for total pages on 120M rows per request; use an estimate or omit. Not cache pages of a moving list.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sort by a non-indexed column (total)? -> Add (total, id) index for that sort or restrict sort options.
  • Backwards paging? -> Flip the comparison and order, then reverse in the app.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A partner crawler took down a read replica for two hours; cursor pagination dropped the same crawl from 9 hours of DB time to 4 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scales hardware.
  • Hire: Explains OFFSET cost and moves to keyset.
  • Strong hire: Tiebreaker column, composite index, API trade-offs, rate limiting and count handling.

questions.promptHtml: Is a CTE an optimization fence? How did Postgres change in version 12, and when would you force materialization?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many engineers assume CTEs always run once; this causes both missed optimizations and unexpected recomputation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Before Postgres 12 every CTE was materialized, so filters from the outer query were not pushed into it. From 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined like a subquery; one referenced multiple times is materialized by default. I can override with MATERIALIZED or NOT MATERIALIZED. I force MATERIALIZED when the CTE is expensive and used several times, or to stop the planner from picking a bad plan; I use NOT MATERIALIZED to allow predicate pushdown."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
PG <= 11 : CTE = fence, computed fully once
PG >= 12 : single-reference, non-recursive -> inlined; multi-reference -> materialized
  • Inlined CTE can use indexes with outer WHERE conditions.
  • Materialized CTE has no statistics from the base table, so row estimates can be poor, but it guarantees a single evaluation.
  • Data-modifying CTEs (INSERT ... RETURNING) always execute exactly once.
  • MySQL 8 merges simple CTEs like derived tables or materializes them depending on use (verify against the version).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
WITH recent AS NOT MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created > now() - interval '30 days'
)
SELECT * FROM recent WHERE customer_id = 42;        -- customer_id filter can be pushed in

WITH big AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT customer_id, sum(total) s FROM orders GROUP BY 1)
SELECT * FROM big a JOIN big b ON a.s = b.s AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a CTE is a temp table that is always computed once.
  • Using a CTE as a "hint" on Postgres 12+ without the keyword.
  • Using the same expensive CTE logic twice by copy-paste instead of referencing it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a materialized CTE be slower? -> Full result is built even if the outer query needs a few rows.
  2. Why is a recursive CTE always iterative? -> It is evaluated using a work table loop.
  3. How to confirm in a plan? -> CTE Scan indicates materialization; absent means inlined.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "CTEs are for readability". The senior knows the version change and uses MATERIALIZED as a deliberate tool.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After an upgrade from PG 11 to 14, a report got 20x faster because its CTE inlined; a different one slowed down because it was now computed three times and needed MATERIALIZED. Both were found by comparing EXPLAIN before and after.

questions.contextHtml:
A category-tree endpoint uses a recursive CTE to list all descendants of a category. After a bulk import, the endpoint hangs; Postgres shows one backend at 100% CPU for 12 minutes, temp files growing to 40 GB, then the disk alarm fires.

WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id FROM categories c JOIN t ON c.parent_id = t.id
) SELECT * FROM t;

The table has 80k rows. Investigation: category 514 has parent_id = 9120 and 9120's ancestor chain loops back to 514. Red herring: a vacuum was running.
questions.promptHtml: How did one small table consume 40 GB, and how do you fix and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Kill it and restart", with no prevention, or tuning work_mem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the data supposed to be a tree? Who writes parent_id? Is the endpoint user-triggered?
  2. Immediate mitigation: pg_cancel_backend(pid), set statement_timeout on the API role, free the temp space, fix the cyclic rows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A cycle with UNION ALL never reaches an empty frontier; the work table grows forever. Or a very deep legitimate tree (80k rows cannot yield 40 GB without a loop).
  4. How I'd verify each: Run a cycle detection query with a depth bound:
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, ARRAY[id] path FROM categories
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, t.path || c.id FROM categories c JOIN t ON c.id = t.parent_id
  WHERE NOT c.id = ANY(t.path))
SELECT id FROM t WHERE parent_id = path[1];   -- ancestors that point back to the start: a cycle

Also check pg_stat_activity and temp file counters. 5. Root cause: A cycle in parent_id data plus UNION ALL: each iteration re-emits the same rows indefinitely. 6. Fix: Short term break the loop (UPDATE categories SET parent_id = NULL WHERE id = 514). Make the query self-protecting:

WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, 1 AS depth FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, t.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN t ON c.parent_id = t.id
  WHERE t.depth < 20
) CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path     -- Postgres 14+
SELECT * FROM t WHERE NOT is_cycle;

Long term, prevent loops at write time with a trigger or use ltree/closure tables. 7. Prevention: statement_timeout and temp_file_limit; data validation job; test with a cyclic fixture. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not switch to UNION as the only guard (it dedupes and stops loops but pays a sort/hash and hides bad data). Not raise limits. A depth cap of 20 must exceed the real maximum depth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does UNION stop the loop? -> Duplicate rows are discarded, so the frontier eventually empties.
  • Deep hierarchies read often? -> Closure table or materialized path for O(1) subtree lookups.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A one-row data fix by support created a loop in an org chart and filled a temp volume, taking down every query that needed sort space.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises memory or restarts.
  • Hire: Spots the cycle and adds a depth cap.
  • Strong hire: Uses CYCLE/path tracking, temp_file_limit, timeouts and write-time prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
A customer listing shows last order date and total spent via correlated subqueries:

SELECT c.id, c.name,
  (SELECT max(created) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS last_order,
  (SELECT sum(total)   FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS spent
FROM customers c WHERE c.city = 'Pune';

Today: 20k Pune customers, 5M orders, 120 ms. Growth plan: 10x customers and orders. orders(customer_id) has an index. The query is run for every segment page load. Excerpt for current plan (illustrative):

-- illustrative
SubPlan 1  (actual time=0.004..0.004 loops=20000)
SubPlan 2  (actual time=0.012..0.012 loops=20000)

Customers in the biggest segment have 5,000+ orders each.
questions.promptHtml: Will it hold at 10x? What do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It's fine, there is an index" or rewrites to JOIN without grouping, creating fan-out.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How skewed are orders per customer? Is exact freshness required? How often is it run?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed today; set up metrics.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: At 10x: 200k probes x 2 subplans; each aggregate over 500+ rows (more for heavy customers) means 200k x 500 = 100M row reads. The two subplans also repeat work (two scans per customer).
  4. How I'd verify each: Load-test with scaled data; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and watch buffer hits.
  5. Root cause: Cost is roughly customers x orders-per-customer for aggregates; nothing precomputes per-customer results.
  6. Fix: Single pass aggregation, combining both measures:
SELECT c.id, c.name, a.last_order, a.spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, max(created) last_order, sum(total) spent FROM orders GROUP BY 1) a
  ON a.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.city = 'Pune';

For many segments, maintain customer_stats incrementally (updated at order write, or refreshed by a matview). Add a covering index (customer_id) INCLUDE (created, total) for index-only scans. 7. Prevention: Capacity test at 10x data before launch; track query p95 with scale. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The pre-aggregating subquery scans all 50M orders even for 200k Pune customers; the planner may push customer_id through only for simple cases. For a small segment, LATERAL or the correlated form is better. I'd choose by selectivity: small segments use LATERAL; big segments use grouping or a summary table.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Needs real-time exactness? -> Increment stats in the same transaction as the order.
  • Why not a window function? -> It keeps all rows; here we want one row per customer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A segment page grew from 0.2 s to 14 s in a year; a summary table brought it to 30 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Says it scales linearly with no analysis.
  • Hire: Computes cost and uses single-pass aggregation.
  • Strong hire: Chooses by selectivity, covering index, summary table, and freshness trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: How does a database execute a window function, what does it cost, and can an index help?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows whether you understand windows as sort-plus-scan operations, not magic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The engine sorts the input by partition keys then order keys, then streams through it computing the function per row with a frame. So cost is dominated by the sort, O(n log n), and memory for the frame state. An index whose columns match PARTITION BY then ORDER BY can supply sorted input and skip the sort. Window results cannot be filtered in WHERE; you wrap them in a subquery."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
scan -> Sort(partition cols, order cols) -> WindowAgg (per-partition state) -> project
  • Several windows with different PARTITION/ORDER need several sorts; reuse the same window definition (WINDOW w AS (...)) so one sort serves many functions.
  • Big partitions with frames like UNBOUNDED PRECEDING for aggregates use running state, O(1) per row; unbounded frames on last_value or a RANGE with many peers can add cost.
  • Filtering: engines (Postgres 15+) can add a Run Condition for row_number() <= N or monotonic functions to stop early (verify version); older ones compute everything.
  • An index on (customer_id, created DESC) lets row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created DESC) avoid the explicit sort; a pre-filter in WHERE reduces rows first.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created DESC);
EXPLAIN SELECT id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created DESC) FROM orders;
-- illustrative: WindowAgg -> Index Scan using orders_customer_id_created_idx   (no Sort node)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Many windows with different orderings, each adding a sort.
  • Forgetting a WHERE to shrink input before the window.
  • Expecting LIMIT to make the window cheap; the whole partition set is processed first (except run conditions).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a window not reduce rows? -> It annotates rows; GROUP BY collapses.
  2. External sort? -> If it exceeds work_mem, it spills to disk.
  3. Window vs self-join for running totals? -> Window is O(n log n); a self-join is O(n^2).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer describes syntax. The senior explains sort cost, shared window definitions, index alignment and spill risks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard with five windows of different orderings sorted 40M rows five times; unifying the window definition cut runtime by 60%.
